title_en: A Natural Gas Project Off Alaska’s Coast May Be a Russian Ploy for Intel on the Arctic
excerpt_en: The post A Natural Gas Project Off Alaska’s Coast May Be a Russian Ploy for Intel on the Arctic appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: A collage showing a diagram of the key parameters of the proposed terminal, a photo of a U.S. Navy exercise in the Beaufort Sea in 2022, and two vantage points on the Trans-Alaska Pipeline System. Photo illustration by Lisa Larson-Walker/ProPublica. Photos by Lance King/Getty Images, Justin Yarborough/U.S. Navy. To an outsider, the research boats bobbing in the frigid and stormy Beaufort Sea off Alaska would seem little cause for alarm. Oil and gas companies have regularly explored the area for decades.

For this project, businessmen from the United Arab Emirates were touting a plan to tap the vast natural gas reserves that lay beneath the tundra of Alaska’s North Slope. They promised the operation would eventually be American-owned. No one could dispute Alaska’s dire energy needs — not to mention the potential for lucrative exports.

The surveyors last year used specialized equipment to map the depth and shape of the seabed, collect samples of shallow marine sediments and conduct sonar scans to check for obstructions such as shipwrecks. Documents show that their work was not far, as the crow flies, from the start of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline System — a cornerstone of U.S. energy production. An Air Force long-range radar station sat just to the west. More than 100 miles off the coast, the Navy’s fast-attack nuclear submarines sometimes practiced surfacing through the thick Arctic ice.

But this project was far from routine. While the contractors performing the work were American, the UAE company paying for the surveys was actually being steered by Russia’s liquefied natural gas giant, Novatek — a company under partial U.S. sanctions, documents and interviews show.

The proposal to create an LNG processing plant on Alaska’s coast has already put reams of scientific data about the strategically critical region within reach of Novatek’s leader, an oligarch who is close to President Vladimir Putin, a ProPublica investigation found.

The Financial Times and The New York Times reported on the Russian ties to the venture last month. But the extent to which the company gathered detailed information about sensitive areas of Alaska has not been previously disclosed.

Such information is highly valuable in the ever-changing and unpredictable Arctic, with its potential routes for both naval ships and missiles. Norwegian security services and U.S. lawmakers have expressed concerns this year about the danger of increased spy and sabotage operations by Russia in the Arctic.

Russia-backed information gathering so close to the U.S. shoreline can be seen as “a direct challenge to sovereignty and security,” said Heather Conley, a former State Department official who is now a senior fellow with the American Enterprise Institute.
“It’s super, super sensitive,” she said, adding, “Any scientific data, it immediately is dual use,” meaning it can serve both military and civilian ends.

Information on changing sea ice and other conditions off the North Slope could help Russia plan activities that undermine U.S. security, said Troy Bouffard, director of the Center for Arctic Security and Resilience at the University of Alaska, Fairbanks. The fact that the surveys were given permits and done without interference could be seen as an intelligence failure, he said.
Bouffard added that it’s “highly unlikely” that intelligence personnel didn’t learn of the effort because any work in the austere, remote and militarily sensitive North Slope area stands out.
“All this is really surprising,” Bouffard said. “Should not have happened.”

The surveys were conducted in the second half of 2025, paused during harsh weather, then restarted in mid-2026, documents and sources say. By late August 2026, dozens of contractors were stationed on three large vessels — the Annika Marie, the Ukpik and the Uŋalaq — loaded with equipment for tasks such as monitoring waves, testing currents, and tides, and drilling core samples in the mud, according to a person familiar with the situation.

Then, in September, the CEO of the project’s U.S. arm, Polar Train LNG, resigned, questioned the operation’s legality and asserted it was a Russian ploy to gain control of a strategic U.S. asset, Alaska’s natural gas reserves.

In 2025, the survey work was focused on an area just west of Prudhoe Bay, which is near where the pipeline originates, documents and sources say. The next year, as the area thawed, Polar Train’s CEO, Joel Riddle, and his team told his financiers that location was not ideal for an LNG operation because of the high cost of dredging that would be needed and the potential to interfere with whaling by local residents. They urged the company’s UAE parent to focus on a site more than 250 miles to the west.

A page from a Tech Wave presentation on plans to locate a liquified natural gas operation in Alaska. Polar Train LNG is a subsidiary of UAE-based Tech Wave. Reviewed by ProPublica But the UAE company asserted its control over the purportedly American outfit Riddle led in late August and ordered the contractors offshore to head back to a site closer to Prudhoe Bay. Riddle resigned the next month, on Sept. 19, warning that Polar Train’s “investments” were “very likely sooner or later to trigger” a federal inquiry.

Polar Train had applied to the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control the month before, seeking a waiver of U.S. sanctions to allow it to purchase a partially built LNG plant sitting in a Murmansk, Russia, shipyard and transport it to Alaska.

“Deploying this technology in Alaska serves not only to unlock U.S. LNG resources in the Pacific basin closer to key export markets in Asia,” said the application, which ProPublica obtained, “but also to ensure this cutting-edge equipment is deployed primarily to the benefit of the United States rather than Russia.”

title_en: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy says Putin ‘lives in a different reality’ as Abu Dhabi talks get under way
excerpt_en: Ukrainian president dismisses Moscow’s claims of gains in Donbas region but says first day of trilateral talks were constructive. What we know on day 1,722
body_en: Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the US has backed Ukraine’s assessment of what is happening on the battlefield and that Vladimir Putin lives in a “different reality”, as American-led trilateral discussions between Ukraine, ⁠Russia and the US got under way in Abu Dhabi. In a post on social media, Zelenskyy said that Russia has claimed at the talks that they occupied half of the Donbas in Ukraine’s east. “This is the problem. Putin lives in a different reality,” the Ukrainian president wrote, adding “I can draw a picture for him too where I fully occupy Russia. But it’s not true. What was good is that the American side confirmed the Ukrainian assessment of what is happening on the battlefield.”

Zelenskyy said he was “happy” to see a change in the approach by US mediators at the Abu Dhabi talks. “I see changes. I’m very happy with what I hear. We will see what can be done,” Zelenskyy told a press conference in Copenhagen after being asked about changes in the approach to peace talks made by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff.

Zelenskyy described the first day of talks – the first three-sided discussions to be held since February – as constructive and substantive. He said the agenda in Abu Dhabi had included formulating a new security architecture for Europe, an idea raised earlier on Tuesday by Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov. “We are all very cautious with this topic because nobody really understands 100% what they want. I think we understand, but nobody saw the documents, what the Americans discussed with the Russians,” Zelenskyy said.

In Abu Dhabi, US officials have said they are seeking a “final end” to the war, Andrew Roth and Jennifer Rankin report. Part of the Trump administration’s proposal involves drawing up a new “long-term security architecture” between Russia and Europe, administration officials have said, but European officials are concerned that Russia may stick to its hardline demands that Nato should roll back its military footprint across eastern Europe, which would threaten to leave allies vulnerable to Moscow’s influence.

Ukraine’s foreign minister said he ⁠had urged US secretary of state Marco Rubio to accelerate ⁠interceptor deliveries as Russia ramps up attacks on energy ⁠infrastructure. Speaking to Reuters after talks with Rubio, Andrii Sybiha said he had pressed Washington to maintain pressure on Moscow even as diplomatic efforts to end the war took ‌place in Abu Dhabi. He said Ukraine remained prepared to discuss a range of de-escalatory measures, including ceasefires covering the Black Sea and energy infrastructure.

Friedrich Merz has signalled he will block the EU’s seven-year budget unless there is a deal on financial aid for Ukraine, triggering accusations of “typical blackmail” from some other European leaders and setting the stage for stormy talks later this month, Jennifer Rankin reports from Brussels. The German chancellor’s intervention has angered leaders in central Europe who are net beneficiaries of EU funds but do not want to take part in an upcoming funding round to support Ukraine’s war effort. “What the chancellor is doing is typical blackmail, and I will not give in to it,” Slovakia’s Russia-friendly prime minister, Robert Fico, told reporters in Bratislava, alongside his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babiš.

Latvia ⁠and Lithuania warned people across several regions to take shelter due ⁠to threats ⁠of unidentified drones entering their airspace via neighbouring Russia or Belarus early on Wednesday. Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Centre said its warning included ⁠the country’s second city of Kaunas, which has a population of about ‌300,000 people. As ‌Ukraine attacks Russia’s Baltic Sea oil shipping ports, some of its drones have missed their targets and led to security warnings in neighbouring countries. Moscow ⁠has accused Kyiv of using Nato airspace as cover for attacks, while Kyiv says some of its drones have been steered off ‌course by Russian signal jamming. The Nato countries blame Russia for the incidents, saying it ignited the war.

title_en: Bank of England’s inflation response ‘risks higher interest rates for longer’
excerpt_en: Thinktank Niesr says timid rate rise last week likely to make inflation more persistent feature of UK economy
body_en: The Bank of England is risking higher interest rates for longer after a hesitant response to rising inflation, according to leading thinktank.

In a searing critique of the central bank’s tactics, the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (Niesr) said a timid increase in interest rates last week was likely to mean inflation staying above the Bank’s 2% target until at least 2030.
The thinktank said inflation was likely to become a more persistent feature of the UK economy unless the Bank took tougher action.
The Bank’s monetary policy committee increased the cost of borrowing from 3.75% to 4% last week and hinted at another increase to combat inflationary pressure unleashed by the Iran war.

The director of the Niesr, David Aikman, urged the Bank of England to be more aggressive in tackling inflation, saying all the ingredients were in place for workers to demand inflation-linked salary rises.
“Inflation is set to rise above 4% in the new year, just as most pay awards for 2027 are being agreed, so the risk that it becomes embedded is rising.
“One further quarter-point rise is unlikely to be enough, and the longer the MPC waits, the more it will eventually need to do.”

UK inflation stands at 3.5%, well above the Bank’s 2% target, driven higher by the soaring cost of fuel. Oil and gas prices have risen sharply since the end of February, when the US and Israel launched their war on Iran.

Brent crude oil has persistently traded at more than $100 a barrel in recent weeks – compared with about $70 before the war – but on Tuesday it traded below $90 at one point, the lowest since 31 August, after Donald Trump downplayed the need for military action against Iran “at this point”.

Investors, however, reined in their enthusiasm after US inflation climbed by 0.4 percentage points from September to October, revealing that high oil and gas prices were continuing to drive up costs. The S&P 500 index of leading US companies was down 0.9% by early afternoon on Wall Street.

The Niesr said its forecasts for growth in the UK and the global economy were based on oil prices at $105 a barrel. However, it cautioned that while prices had dropped, continued difficulties shipping and refining meant consumer prices would decline slowly.
Stephen Millard, an economist at the institute, said the lower oil price was also dependent on Trump sticking to his new policy. “We’ve seen him change his mind before,” he said.

The Niesr expects the UK economy to grow by 1.6% this year, but by only 0.9% in 2028 as high inflation, high interest rates and tight government spending take a toll on consumer and business confidence.

The chancellor, John Healey, was criticised for deferring difficult decisions in the budget last month, which the institute said would leave a £30bn hole in the government’s finances if the pattern of doing so over the last decade was repeated next year.

Aikman said financial markets would punish the Treasury by raising the price of loans to the UK if it became clear that government spending was going to soar in areas such as defence without savings being made elsewhere.
He said there was a “double whammy” from higher energy prices and rising global borrowing costs that was not being addressed.
“Those pressures reflect global developments and cannot be avoided,” he said. “How monetary and fiscal policy respond to them is a domestic choice, and on both fronts decisions are being deferred.”

title_en: US justice department sues Lyft over alleged refusal to serve passengers with disabilities
excerpt_en: Lawsuit filed in California claims drivers routinely refuse to transport individuals with service animals or mobility devices
body_en: The Department of Justice sued Lyft on Monday, accusing the ride-share giant of discrimination for denying service to passengers with disabilities.

The federal lawsuit, which was filed in the US district court for the northern district of California, said Lyft drivers have routinely refused to transport individuals who depend on service animals or use mobility devices, such as wheelchairs, an alleged violation of the Americans With Disabilities Act (ADA).

In one example, provided in the complaint, a Nevada woman who uses a wheelchair, due to injuries from a near-fatal car accident, had a Lyft driver allegedly drive away, as she waved to catch his attention.
A Texas man who has vision and hearing impairments began to leave his guide dog at home, despite the challenges of navigating, to avoid further service denials, according to the suit.
The justice department accused Lyft of being privy to “widespread disability-based discrimination” on its platform, but failing to take action to prevent the alleged mistreatment.

“Individuals with disabilities should be able to rely on rideshare services free of discrimination,” said Jesus A Osete, acting assistant attorney general, in a statement. “We intend to uphold the ADA’s promise that people with disabilities are entitled to equal access in every part of public life, including essential transportation services.”
Lyft firmly rejected the accusations in a statement.

The lawsuit is the latest from the federal government that targets ride-hailing companies for treatment of would-be riders with disabilities. The administration filed a similar lawsuit against Uber last year, which is ongoing. Uber settled a separate suit in 2022, and Lyft settled a different one in 2020. The companies stress that their policies and in-app tools require that drivers provide ADA accommodations and remind them of the consequences of refusing to do so.

Lyft policies require drivers to accommodate riders who travel with service animals or mobility devices, and “drivers who violate these policies face serious consequences, including permanent deactivation”, the company said in a statement.
“We’ve cooperated with the DOJ throughout its review and remain committed to serving every rider, including riders with disabilities,” the company said.
The DoJ said it was seeking $53m for individuals who have been discriminated against and have submitted complaints to Lyft or the department.

title_en: Economic coercion once ousted Iran’s leader – but that was the 1950s; don’t expect a repeat today
excerpt_en: A two-year blockade imposed on Iran by Britain gave way to a coup and leadership change. But seven decades later, circumstances are very different.
body_en: Pro-monarchists celebrate after the 1953 Iranian coup. Intercontinentale/AFP via Getty Images “Very little gets into, or out of, Iran!” President Donald Trump claimed on Nov. 8, 2026, in a social media post that also lauded “history’s greatest Naval Blockade.”

It followed the unveiling of Task Force Iron Gate – the Trump administration’s latest plan to isolate the Iranian economy in a bid to coerce the government in Tehran to bend to Washington’s will. At the same time, Trump has suggested that a return to open war with Iran is “highly unlikely.”

From my perspective as an expert on Iran’s relations with the wider world, I believe that the U.S. war in Iran – now into its ninth month – is increasingly resembling an earlier episode of Iranian-Western conflict. In the early 1950s, the British imposed a two-year blockade and embargo against Iran after Iran’s then-prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh, nationalized the country’s U.K.-controlled oil industry.
These efforts culminated in a 1953 British- and American-backed plot to stir up protest in Iran and eventually overthrow Mossadegh.

Seventy-three years later, many of those themes – oil, economic coercion, political intervention – ring true again. Trump’s stated and shifting justifications for the war include imminent threat preemption and nuclear nonproliferation. Yet his main motivations seem to be choosing Iran’s leader and controlling its oil.

Having failed to achieve this through direct military force, Trump’s main means for achieving the objectives are now a naval blockade and economic isolation – much like the British some seven decades earlier.

But there the analogy may end. Unlike during the Mossadegh era, Iran has shown it can fight back against foreign intervention and coercive economic actions through asymmetric warfare and economic disruption.

From oil nationalization … In March 1951, one month before becoming prime minister and while serving as a parliamentary representative, Mossadegh persuaded the Iranian parliament to pass legislation that nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company. While popular with many Iranians, who perceived it as a long overdue measure to reclaim the nation’s independence and control its wealth, the move was considered by the British a breach of contract and a theft of its largest overseas asset.

The U.K. filed complaints with the newly created United Nations Security Council. But in July of that year, negotiations stalled and tensions escalated between Mossadegh – now the prime minister – and the British.

Economic coercion began with the British obstructing Iran’s oil sales by informing Iranian tankers that their receipts – issued when cargo is loaded on board – would not be accepted on the international market. In August, the U.K. stepped up the campaign by imposing a naval blockade against Iran.

In the process, they intercepted oil tankers off the Persian coast and prevented Iran from exporting petroleum to other countries. The British also prohibited the export of key commodities to Iran – such as sugar and steel – and froze Iranian bank accounts and assets in the U.K.
That same month, the U.K. evacuated its British technicians and closed Anglo-Iranian Oil Company refineries and other installations in the city of Abadan.

Mossadegh and his government assumed they could replace the technicians with those from other countries while training Iranians to fill the void. However, through legal threats and agreements, the British convinced other international oil companies in the United States and Europe, except Italy, to refrain from sending personnel.

… to Operation Ajax Due to the British blockade and embargo, Iran’s petroleum production declined by about 96% and its oil income to almost zero between 1950 and 1952. At the same time, foreign oil companies like British Petroleum and Saudi Aramco doubled their production to offset the economic impact to the U.K. and the world of reduced or nonexistent production and exports from Iran.

Amid the economic crisis, Mossadegh’s inability to alleviate poverty, among other issues, caused his political coalition to fracture and fueled the British and American propaganda campaign against him ahead of his overthrow in Operation Ajax on Aug. 19, 1953.

A year later, the Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, consolidated power and signed an oil agreement with the British. In it, Iran’s share of the profits increased slightly, while an overwhelming majority of between 75% and 79% continued to be claimed by British and American companies. In exchange, the British lifted the blockade and enabled Iran to resume exporting oil on the international market.

The difference of deterrence The U.K.’s campaign to pressure Iran and oust its leader contains parallels with the current conflict. Now, just as then, a Western power is hoping to bring Iranian leadership to its knees – and encourage widespread anti-government protests – through coercive economic actions.
But contrary to the 1950s, Tehran today is better placed to deter its foreign adversary.

While Washington has drastically degraded Iran’s conventional military capabilities, including its air force and navy, Tehran has effectively employed drones, missiles and proxies to repeatedly strike U.S. assets in the region. Back in the 1950s, Iran had no network of sympathetic regional militias like it has today, and it lacked the sufficient technology to hit back at a conventionally superior military.

Iran can also counter economic measures. Since the war began in February 2026, Tehran and its partners have continuously targeted the tanker traffic and civilian and energy infrastructure of the Arab Gulf states.
Consequently, it has caused Gulf kingdoms to rethink remaining under the U.S. security umbrella and diversify defense partnerships to include other powers inside and outside the region.

title_en: UN chief urges Cop31 hosts Turkey and Australia to turn fossil fuel promises into action
excerpt_en: António Guterres calls for ‘clear next steps’ as countries face pressure to agree concrete measures
body_en: Turkey and Australia, the co-hosts of crucial climate talks, must urgently move from discussing the end of fossil fuels to delivering it, the UN chief has said.

“It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable,” António Guterres said, in a dramatic intervention on the second day of the conference on Tuesday.
“Now, here at Cop31, we must move from discussing the transition to organising it, financing it, and delivering it.”

The two countries hosting Cop31 are significant exporters of fossil fuels. Early on Tuesday, the Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, was extolling his country’s oilfields even as he prepared for his appearance at the summit on Wednesday.

Guterres said the talks should end with “clear next steps” to advance a roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels presented to delegates on Tuesday by Brazil, which presided over last year’s talks.

During a presentation with the Brazilians, Guterres – who will step down as UN secretary general at the end of this year and has made the climate crisis a central part of his agenda, often intervening on issues with dramatic language – was energetically backed by the former US secretary of state and climate envoy John Kerry, the UN’s chief climate negotiator, Simon Stiell, and his predecessor, the Mexican diplomat Patricia Espinosa. He was met by rapturous applause as he left the stage.

Brazil announced at the close of last year’s Cop30 climate summit that it would produce the roadmap. Previewing it last week, the country said an exit from fossil fuels would boost economies and help pull people out of poverty.
Kerry said the roadmap had come “at a critical moment” but “words in conversation don’t cut a single ton of emissions – action does”.

There is growing pressure on this Cop to deliver after several years in which the summits have been criticised for a lack of progress. It took 28 years of annual UN Cop negotiations for the first mention of a transition away from fossil fuels to be included in a final decision, at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023.

Greta Thunberg, the Swedish climate activist who inspired global climate protests several years ago, attended this year’s Cop for the first time since 2021,. “Cops have become greenwashed circuses. That is the reality,” she told reporters.

The drama came on the eve of a two-day leaders’ summit at which more than 90 world leaders, including the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, his Australian counterpart, Anthony Albanese, and the newly elected Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, were expected to speak and join negotiations.

Alden Meyer, a senior associate at the climate thinktank E3G and a Cop veteran, described the presentation of the roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels as “an incredible display of collective firepower”.

“There’s clearly now an expectation that the presidencies [of Australia and Turkey] will pick up the baton from Brazil in some way,” he said. “But it won’t be agreed by consensus here. It took us 28 Cop meetings to get the need to transition away from fossil fuels into a Cop decision.

“This is what we are getting down to and it will be interesting to see how this hybrid presidency responds to this. This is the challenge to this presidency and how they pick up this baton and keep this discussion going.”

A spokesperson for Australia’s climate minister, Chris Bowen, said: “Our message had been clear: countries working together is not only the best way, it is the only way of dealing with climate change and the other crises that countries are facing.
“Before us is the opportunity to make our nations more prosperous, our energy system more secure and the climate more safe.”
The Turkish hosts were approached for comment.

The second day of the conference also saw more than 700 groups, ranging from trade unions to disability advocates, urging diplomats to prioritise a “just transition” for the people who will be hit hardest by a shift to a clean economy.

Organisations from 88 countries demanded a mechanism at Cop31 to turn promises of a just transition into action. Known as the Belém-Antalya Mechanism (BAM), it would seek to support issues including human rights, gender equality and good jobs, while respecting Indigenous rights.

Lidy Nacpil, the coordinator of the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development, said: “Workers and communities, especially in the global south, welcomed and celebrated the Cop30 decision to develop a just transition mechanism – or BAM – which has the promise of delivering real support and action for just transition on the ground.

“However, in pre-Cop, governments of the global north have once again exposed their determination to pour cold water over this promise, by limiting what a mechanism can do and delaying the process of its operationalisation.”
On Tuesday, with 100,000 people attending the talks, many delegates were stuck in traffic for hours. Tram services were crammed with attenders, while some bus journeys took more than three hours.

title_en: The Garbage Man: Bill Gates Has Earned Billions Investing in Climate-Polluting Landfills
excerpt_en: The post The Garbage Man: Bill Gates Has Earned Billions Investing in Climate-Polluting Landfills appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Mark Harris for ProPublica. Source images: Getty Images, RMI. In November 2015, world leaders descended on Paris to negotiate a historic agreement to limit global warming. But on the summit’s opening day, attention turned to a private citizen slouched awkwardly in a chair on stage: Bill Gates.

Gates, with his characteristic flop of sandy hair, grinned impishly as President Barack Obama called him a “visionary” and a “driving force” behind a pair of pledges that both saw as key to the larger agreement. First the world’s largest economies would double their spending on research into clean-energy technologies. Then investors like Gates would back the startups that emerged. The Microsoft cofounder had already enlisted two dozen other billionaires to join the effort.
For Gates, who’d become increasingly consumed by this unprecedented threat to human well-being, the moment marked his arrival as a leading figure in the fight against climate change.

“If we back over 50 different breakthrough approaches, we know that several of those will give us the solution that we need,” Gates said during his own speech. He would invest at least $2 billion of his own money in companies developing geothermal wells, new kinds of nuclear reactors and machines that pull carbon from the air, to name just a few.

With much less fanfare, however, Gates has put more than double that amount into a very dirty, old-school industry. At the time of the Paris summit, he was already the dominant shareholder of America’s No. 2 landfill operator, Republic Services. He has since increased his stake to 38% of the company, a position worth $29 billion.

Bill Gates’ Stake in Republic Services, a Landfill Operator, Now Exceeds a Fifth of His Net Worth Note: “Other” includes stakes in other publicly traded companies and accumulated dividends and investment returns. Sources: Forbes’ The World’s Billionaires, Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index, SEC filings, StockAnalysis.com Chris Alcantara/ProPublica While fossil fuels get most of the attention, scientists increasingly see landfills as a crucial climate issue. They’re responsible for as much as a fifth of the country’s emissions of methane, a highly potent greenhouse gas, studies show. Republic alone generates as much climate pollution as 3 million gasoline-burning cars each year, according to its own reports.

One might imagine that a landfill operator with Gates as its largest shareholder — and with three people closely linked to Gates on its board — would lead the way in tackling those emissions. Even after seemingly softening his stance on global warming in a controversial blog post last year, Gates remains one of the world’s most prominent voices on the issue. As he did in his bestselling 2021 book “How to Avoid a Climate Disaster,” he continues to advocate for cutting emissions, and he has called on his fellow business leaders to do their part.

Gates, though, has failed to make Republic live up to his own climate principles, a ProPublica investigation has found. Federal inspectors have repeatedly found methane escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits. The company has refrained from adopting the ambitious emissions-reduction goal embraced by its main competitor. Republic has even lobbied against policies that could make the wider industry cleaner, including by keeping organic waste out of landfills in the first place.

“It seems very likely that Bill Gates has the power to influence Republic’s behavior to make it more climate-friendly, even if that costs the company profits,” said Ann Lipton, a legal scholar who studies corporate governance at the University of Colorado, Boulder.
As for whether he should, in her words, “put his money where his mouth is,” Lipton said, “you can leave it to the reader to make the moral judgment.”

Gates’ Climate Awakening Gates didn’t respond to repeated requests to discuss his landfill investments, and ProPublica couldn’t find any public comments he’s made about them. But the bet has proven wildly lucrative. Since November 1999, when he emerged as the owner of 5% of Republic’s shares — “ It’s ‘Garbage In’ for Gates,” the New York Post headline read — the company’s stock price has soared thirtyfold. And Gates has personally received $2.6 billion in dividends, a ProPublica analysis of securities filings shows.

In those early days, Gates hadn’t yet awakened to the threat of global warming. It was a different time. Microsoft Windows ran on more than 80% of personal computers. Gates was the world’s richest person, and his bespectacled face graced the cover of Time magazine twice that year. He was simultaneously criticized for what a federal judge determined to be Microsoft’s monopolistic practices and admired for establishing what was soon to become the world’s largest charitable foundation.

A rare clue to why Gates made his foray into landfills can be found in an interview he gave to Fortune that year. To fund his plan to give away virtually his entire fortune, he said he’d given his personal money manager, Michael Larson, a simple remit: Sell Microsoft shares, buy safe, boring assets.

Republic’s then-chairman, billionaire Wayne Huizenga, had flown Larson by helicopter to his private golf course in Florida, according to the article. It’s unclear if Huizenga pitched Republic there, but it fit the remit. America would always produce trash, ensuring a steady stream of revenue. After that initial investment, Larson progressively increased Gates’ stake in Republic over the years that followed. Larson would also acquire a small chunk of Republic’s main competitor, Waste Management — which Huizenga also once led — on behalf of the Gates Foundation.

title_en: Jon Stewart on Trump’s testy 60 Minutes interview: ‘Was that sass?’
excerpt_en: Late-night hosts discussed Trump’s interview with the ‘new, Maga-fied’ CBS program and Stephen Miller’s White House promotion
body_en: Late-night hosts reacted to Donald Trump ’s strange interview with 60 Minutes and his unpopular promotion of Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff.

Jon Stewart A week after Democrats’ decisive victories in the US midterm elections, widely seen as a repudiation of Trump, Jon Stewart checked in with the beleaguered president. “Donald Trump headed over to the newly Maga-fied CBS for a little self-soothing with one of 60 Minutes’s new correspondents, a religious conservative by the name of Ross Douthat,” he said on Monday’s Daily Show.
On the once-storied news program, Trump claimed that “we have created wealth at a level that our country has never seen before” – “including for yourself,” Douthat cut in.
“Young man, was that sass?” Stewart laughed. “Did the new Maga-fied CBS 60 Minutes just deliver sass to Donald Trump? I think you’re supposed to ‘yes, and … ’ not ‘yes, but … ’.”
Related: Seth Meyers on Republicans: ‘Furiously backpedalling away from Trump’
Trump tried to defend himself, claiming that “everyone’s” wealth increased, but Douthat again countered: “My net worth did not go up by $3bn.”

“I think I’m going to enjoy this,” Stewart relished. “I did not come into this interview thinking: ‘Uh, I’m going to enjoy this.’ But now, as I am watching this, I am thinking to myself: ‘I am going to enjoy this.’ Let me prepare the table for the feast we are all about to enjoy. As regular viewers of our program know, Donald Trump has a somewhat high regard for his own financial acumen. In fact, not 20 minutes prior, in this very same interview we are watching, Donald Trump said this: ‘I’m really good at money and finances.’”
And yet in the same interview, Trump said of his own fortune: “I guess it’s gone up. I don’t even know.”

“My frustration with reporters is, I wish someone would, like, hammer down on this,” said Stewart. “Trump acts like he’s got all this money squirreled away in some index fund, and it just magically grew. Meanwhile, since the guy has returned to office, he’s made $125m from foreign golf and real-estate schemes, $117m from legal settlements, $636m from selling that bullshit novelty meme coin. He’s gotten $800m from his World Liberty Financial crypto company. Why can’t someone just bring this up to his face?”

Douthat did, in fact, ask Trump about World Liberty Financial, which is partly owned by investors connected to the government of the United Arab Emirates. “I think if I told you that story,” he said, “and it was about the Biden family, if I said Joe Biden is the part-owner of a company and it has all of these investments from the Middle East, you would say that sounds corrupt.”
“I’ll have what he’s having,” Stewart cheered, referencing the famous scene from When Harry Met Sally. “I love that Douthat is forcing Trump to compare himself to the Biden crime family.”
In response to that comparison, Trump claimed the difference was he knew “nothing about” his son’s business.

“My god, Ross, you beautiful bearded bastard,” Stewart cheered. “Do you know what you’ve just done here? Do you have any idea what you just did here? You have made Donald Trump admit that the difference between him and Joe Biden is that Joe Biden is more aware of his surroundings.”

Jimmy Kimmel On Jimmy Kimmel Live!, the host kept track of Trump’s reaction to the midterms landslide, which quickly morphed from accepting the results to questioning the legitimacy of the results. Over the weekend, Trump posted on Truth Social: “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong???”

“This is how it starts,” Kimmel said. “This is how he does a little taste of conspiracy. Nothing too intense, just enough to whet your appetite. And then he feeds it a little more. It grows. The lie gets bigger. He keeps repeating it.

“And then he starts talking about people talking about him claiming the election was rigged, as if there are people other than him claiming the election was rigged,. And before you know it, someone in a Viking helmet is making a toilet out of Nancy Pelosi’s desk. God bless America!”

“I don’t think we’re prepared for the amount of insanity that this drama queen president is about to pump on us,” Kimmel added. “Donald Trump right now is a raccoon in a duffel bag. He’s been cut off at the cankles. And there are two possible paths he can take. The first one is to check out. No more meetings. Lots of trips to Mar-a-Lago. Lots of golf with Natalie running behind the cart. Every once in a while he’ll host a Super Bowl team. That’s the best case scenario.”

But the host also saw a different, much darker future on the horizon. “Scenario number two is he goes nuts. Like Jack Nicholson in The Shining nuts. Everybody who works for him gets the axe. He turns on anybody who might possibly want to succeed him, whether that be Lil Marco or JD Vance. Even his own son. Even if Don Jr decides to run for president, his father will say and do anything he can to destroy him. Because he wants to make sure no one but him will ever live in the White House again. He might knock down the rest of it for all we know.”

title_en: Why is Nvidia so powerful in the AI world, and what could Jensen Huang’s scandal really cost?
excerpt_en: A tech CEO’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy is rocking the AI industry.
body_en: Sean Gallup / Getty Images Jensen Huang, the chief executive and co-founder of chipmaking company Nvidia, recently admitted to an extramarital affair. However, it’s not just a tabloid story: the woman involved, Alice Huang, has been accused of being a Chinese intelligence agent.

Computer chips – specifically the chips used to produce and run artificial intelligence (AI) systems – have become a key front in the United States’ rivalry with China for geopolitical power and influence. The most powerful chips are needed for the most advanced AI, and the US has tried to maintain its edge over China by restricting access to those chips.
While the Chinese government rejects claims of espionage, Alice Huang has reportedly been under investigation by the US for years.
So what’s so special about Nvidia? What’s in it for China? And if Jensen Huang goes down, what else could go down with him?
The world’s biggest AI chip company Nvidia is the world’s biggest supplier of the high-end chips used for AI and data centres, with some estimates putting its market share over 80%.

The now multi-trillion-dollar company got its start making chips called graphic processing units (GPUs), used largely for video games. However, these chips – and their successors – turned out to be ideal for the kind of number-crunching needed for training and using AI models.

Other companies such as Google and AMD have tried to make chips that can compete with Nvidia for speed and efficiency, however neither has been able to displace Nvidia from its dominance of the AI market.
Read more: What is a GPU? An expert explains the chips powering the AI boom, and why they’re worth trillions

Why China may be interested As a consequence, Nvidia has played a key role in the US government’s strategy to stall China’s development of AI. Sales of Nvidia’s most powerful chips to China have been restricted since 2022 – though the restrictions were somewhat relaxed last year.

However, Chinese enterprises have repeatedly tested the boundaries of US sanctions. Southeast Asian companies including Megaspeed, Alice Huang’s former employer, have been accused of buying up Nvidia chips and exporting them into China.
Jensen Huang has lobbied intently for a relaxation of US chip export restrictions, which is being seen in a new light after the revelation of his relationship with Alice Huang.
Skipping the sanctions Trade records indicate over US$3 billion in chips crossed from Singapore to China in a single year, alongside similar volumes from Malaysia.
Selling access to banned Nvidia chips to Chinese companies has also become a growth industry.

Nvidia’s value has soared with the AI boom. However, its share price has fallen after the disclosure of the Huang incident, with some analysts asking whether the company propped up sales figures by ignoring sanctions. It has also been reported that an Nvidia executive leaned on US officials to halt an investigation into the firm’s relationship with Megaspeed.
Regulatory impact Nvidia’s share price tumbled after the affair was revealed.

Now the company is reportedly under criminal investigation. At the same time, US technology regulators are mobilising, with Congress requesting Jensen Huang explain his interactions with Alice Huang, and how Nvidia protects itself against foreign espionage.
If Nvidia is forced to guarantee its chips don’t enter China, its sales pipeline may grind to a halt. And if Nvidia hits trouble, the financial impacts could be much wider.
The AI sector is notorious for the amount of circular financing going on – where companies invest in their own suppliers or customers. Nvidia is a key player in this loop.
Investors are already fretting over whether the enormous amounts of money sunk into AI can ever return profits.
While leading AI model builders Anthropic and OpenAI are moving toward public listings or fresh funding rounds, both face harsh reality checks.
OpenAI has delayed its own planned stock market listing, while Anthropic’s expected share market listing is rumoured to face a “junk bond” rating, meaning it’s a high-risk investment.
Data centre firms too are losing value as they face community pushback and soaring energy costs.

title_en: How women bore the consequences of the First World War in British India
excerpt_en: The ‘tears of womenfolk’ in Punjab became the biggest hurdle to military recruitment by December 1924, according to colonial officials.
body_en: Troops of the 29th Lancers Regiment (Deccan Horse) near Pys in India, armed with lances and making their way through a shell torn landscape, March 1917. (Imperial War Museums) Who do we forget on Remembrance Day?

For a long time, histories of the First World War have been popularly understood in a Euro-centric manner. But descendants of Indian soldiers and researchers have long pushed for recognition for the approximately 1.4 million men from current-day India, Pakistan and Bangladesh who helped wage the First World War for the British Empire.
Yet when it comes to the war’s impact on British India, many of us still think of contributions as military and masculine.
The double portrait of two Sikh risaldars, Jagat Singh and Man Singh, currently on display at the Art Gallery of Ontario is a testament to such recognition.
The men hailed from Punjab, the hub of military recruitment known as the “ sword arm” of the Raj.
The piece was painted in London by Phillip de László two months before the Battle of the Somme in 1916, when many Indian soldiers were wounded or lost their lives.

But remembrance is gendered. Historian Radhika Singha has revealed the overlooked role of non-combatants such as labourers, cooks, sweepers and many other essential “follower” roles in the war. Male and militarized remembrance also takes for granted the impact of the war on those women and families the men left behind.

As my preliminary research into First World War archives of letters, songs and reports indicate, women bore the consequences of the total war thousands of miles away from the Western Front. Early on, women recognized the gendered cost of the war, and were critical of the reliance on their husbands, sons and fathers to wage it.

A recruiting meeting held at one of the hill fairs in India in October 1917. (Press Agency Photographer/India during the First World War, 1914-1918/Imperial War Museums) Compounding gendered hierarchies The impact of the First World War compounded the gendered hierarchies already existing in Punjab.

The state of Punjab in northern India was annexed by the East India Company in 1849. Colonial officials were keen to secure political and economic control by joining hands with existing patriarchs and landowners in this agricultural economy.

First World War Hindi-language recruitment poster with slogan statement that beings: ‘This soldier defends India. He protects his home and family.’ (Imperial War Museum) But such developments were especially harmful for women. As feminist historian Veena Oldenburg has shown, measures such as the codification of customary law based on consultations with male household heads formalized the dominance of the male landowner. This contributed to making women dependent on the men around them.

Colonial officials were also fascinated by the Punjabi peasant because they believed that he embodied war-like qualities. The Darwinian “ martial race theory ” claimed that only certain men in India could be soldiers. Colonial authorities came to view the Punjabi peasant, who worked the land and had a history of a military tradition, as fighting material.

By the turn of the 20th century, these ideas culminated in what researchers termed the “ Punjabization of the Indian Army.” On the eve of the First World War, about 60 per cent of the Indian army was made up of Punjabi men.
When war broke out, colonial authorities promoted recruitment of local men through further promises of land grants, cash rewards and secure pay, and linked it to the ideas of izzat or honour.

How did women respond to the war? While middle class and elite Indian women led campaigns to encourage wives and mothers to send their husbands and sons to war, this response wasn’t universal. Many women in the villages of Punjab tried to prevent their husbands and sons from enlisting.

News and letters from the war front revealed the brutal conditions of trench warfare. According to colonial reports of the time, mothers and wives believed that men were not being adequately trained before they were sent off.

The colonial government denounced such beliefs as wild rumours. Yet historical evidence shows that women in Punjab tried to hinder recruitment efforts to such an extent that, by December 1914, colonial officials complained that the “tears of womenfolk” had become the biggest hurdle to recruitment.
In Amritsar, Punjab, in 1915, an official noted in his diary that women “would trail recruiting parties for several miles, patiently awaiting opportunities to lure away acquired recruits.”

Colonial intelligence reports show women would sing songs blaming King George for taking away their husbands and brothers. In these, women offered trenchant critiques of the colonial government, claiming that their men had been used as fodder by the firangi (colonizer).

In 2016, Berlin based Pakistani artist Bani Abidi displayed contemporary renditions of folk songs at the Edinburgh Art Festival. Entitled, “Memorial to Lost Words,” this exhibition moves beyond “stone engravings or statues” as sites of memory but combines translated letters and folk songs. Phrases from a translated folk song sing:
“Don’t go, don’t go, stay here my friend, the ignorant are packing up and leaving, flowers are withering, friendships are breaking.”

Bani Abidi’s Memorial to Lost Words is a sound installation bearing poignant testament to the tragedy of the First World War. Scrambling for survival Women whose husbands enlisted scrambled for money to survive. Delays in the receipt of remittances and pay added to their economic struggles. A collection of letters shows that one wife wrote to her husband in France that she had only received two months’ worth of allowances in six months and had to resort to pawning her jewellery to “keep myself alive.”
